title: Appopottamax
summary: Appopottamax is recorded as the name of a creek at Bay Shore, mentioned in a Brooklyn Times notice from January 26, 1899. The source also cautions that the name was not otherwise on record and that no other authority had been found for it.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Secatogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Appopottamax matters partly because it is uncertain: the name is recorded from a single later newspaper notice, with a suggested meaning connected to a fishing place by a brook. That caution shows how Native placenames can survive unevenly in print, sometimes as fragments that need careful reading rather than overconfidence. Even so, the Bay Shore creek setting points to a broader South Shore geography of fishing, waterways, and Indigenous place memory.
translation_content:
No documentary variant spellings are given for Appopottamax. If the printed form is correct, the suggested meaning is a place where flags are gathered.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names can intervene in settler colonialism by animating Indigenous history, reminding people of the ancestors of these lands.”

— Yellowhead Institute, Reclaiming Indigenous Place Names (2019), Land use planning and conservation section

Place-name history should show Native people as active and present, not only as names in old documents.
whereintheworld_content: Appopottamax is useful as a cautionary record. It preserves a reported Bay Shore placename while making clear that the source basis is weak and that the location should not be treated as settled without more evidence.
